## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.54074.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.54074.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

We all agree that this work provides a timely transcriptomics dataset that will be of interest to a large number of scientists, and that you and your coauthors did an excellent job with the validation and analysis of these data.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the adult Drosophila ventral nerve cord" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and K VijayRaghavan as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Peter A Sims (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We all agreed that the manuscript is a timely contribution to the Drosophila neuroscience community, with likely implications beyond the fly field. In particular, the authors perform single-cell RNA-seq on ~26k cells from the adult Drosophila ventral nerve cord (VNC). They use clustering analysis to group these cells into 120 distinct clusters, (110 neuronal, 10 non-neuronal). They compare their clusters to known organizing features of the VNC, including developmental lineage, transcription factor enrichment, receptor expression, neurotransmitter identity, and neuropeptide release. Additionally, the authors use Hox gene expression to try to infer spatial origins of sequenced cells. Overall, this paper provides a useful gene expression resource for fly VNC enthusiasts. There are also a handful of interesting biological insights. Altogether, the single cell sequencing approach reveals a new level of organization of the fly VNC and will therefore be of interest to many labs around the world.

However, based on the reviewers' comments, some revisions are required before eLife can offer publication.

Essential revisions:

1) The authors claim to be able to discern specific identifying features about single cells in their dataset, such as spatial distribution (i.e., neuromere identity) and lineage. However, there is no quantitative validation of these claims, only qualitative assessment of a few examples. For ex-ample, the Abstract states, "Cells could also be assigned to specific neuromeres using adult Hox gene expression." Is this really true? Apart from the fact that there is no ground-truth to test this claim from RNA-Seq, the antibody staining of Hox genes is far from "neuromere specific". While there may be a loose relationship between gene expression and spatial location, it does not ap-pear to be sufficient to differentiate between meso and metathoracic with a high degree of certainty. The same pattern seems to be true for lineage identity – in a handful of cases examined in this paper, one can recognize lineages from gene expression. But this is not systematically explored. Readers deserve a more objective sense of what they can infer about single cells from this gene expression dataset. In the absence of a statistical analysis that achieves this, the authors should moderate the claims of the paper and include a more clear discussion about what exactly can be learned about single cells by looking at their gene expression using these methods.

2) The authors state that 28% of cells in their dataset express more than one marker of neuro-transmitter identity, and that this may represent a technical artifact of the single-cell method. This point needs further clarification and discussion. Does this represent contamination? If so, does this provide a means of estimating contamination levels across the entire dataset, assuming that co-expression is not "real"? In addition to citing the antibody staining from Lacin et al., 2019, the authors should use Davis et al., 2020, and Shih et al., 2019, as a points of comparison. Using an alternate technique (TAPIN-seq) that purifies identifies cell-types, these studies find no evidence for co-release in the visual system or the mushroom body.

3) One of the more interesting aspects of the paper is the distribution of neuropeptide-related genes and their remarkably high expression levels. The authors should add a ranked list of npp genes, expression levels, and cognate np-gpcr genes. A similar table is present in the recent paper from Smith et al., 2019. It would also be valuable for the authors to compare their results to those in this recent paper.

4) The authors should more quantitatively compare this dataset to that from the fly brain. Other than transmitter distribution, are there any other major differences? If so, how might these be related to differences in methodology (e.g., drop-seq vs. 10x).

5) The data are presented very much as a resource and the manuscript does not focus on a scientific question or hypotheses. Although the data presented are interesting, relevant, and compelling enough that this should not preclude publication, the authors should add as many conclusions that go beyond this resource perspective as possible. For example, do their data hint at any functional organization of the VNC (e.g. support for the hypothesis that hemilineages are functional units), and can they discuss this a bit more? Are there any other hypotheses for functional units that emerge? How does the amount of cellular diversity compare to the brain? To other organisms? Does their atlas provide any clues as to why there is so much diversity?

6) The main deliverable of these analyses is the clusters they establish in Figure 1 and then use as an organizing scaffold for their more detailed analyses. Clear delineation of these clusters therefore seems very important. I find it vague in the manuscript, however, how the clusters may actually be defined. The authors say that most of the clusters can be identified by unique combinations of marker genes, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 claims to list the "combinations of genes [that] uniquely identify each cluster". But in that figure there are multiple clusters where the same combination of marker genes is listed (e.g. clusters 14, 33, 34, and 78 all list bi and VAChT as the only marker genes defining the cluster). Is that because these clusters are part of a larger "super cluster" (I note 14, 33, 34, and 78 co-localize in their t-SNE plot)? And is the "super cluster" the level at which gene marker combinations are unique? I think articulating the clustering clearly is critical to the paper because that is the level that future scientists will try to compare to morphological cell types. It would also be helpful if there were a large summary table of their many analyses indicating, for each cluster, which lineage, FAN, monamines, peptides, and Hox genes corresponded.

7) Many of the analyses are illustrated with "Chord diagrams". It's not clear what the reader is supposed to take from these diagrams. Are they showing clustering? Are they showing distribution? A quantification of what we are supposed to take from these would be helpful.

8) The authors have four distinguishable replicates in their data set that were each generated by pooling 20 VNCs. However, for essentially all of the analysis, the data from these replicates are pooled and there is a general lack of assessment of consistency across replicates. Figure 1—figure supplement 3A shows the proportional contribution of each replicate to each cluster, but it is impossible to assess any differences in the composition of each replicate from this plot because the replicates are not sub-sampled to the same cell numbers. For example, Replicate 1 contributes only ~5-10% of the total data. Ideally, one would cluster each replicate separately and determine the extent to which the clusters agree with each other across replicates. At the very least, there should be an assessment of the correlation between cluster compositions across replicates based on the current analysis. In addition, the authors should show a tSNE plot where the cells are colored by replicate (rather than by cluster). This should be done for all of the sub-clustering analysis as well.

9) What is the specific rationale for removing cells with fewer than 1,200 UMIs or more than 10,000 UMIs? The authors state that they are trying to remove multiplets with the 10,000 UMI cutoff. Is there evidence from the data that these barcodes are associated with multiplets (e.g. co-expression known mutually exclusive markers)? In general, this approach is somewhat problematic and arbitrary (e.g. see Stoeckius et al., Genome Biology, 2019 for systematic analysis showing the complications of using coverage to identify multiplets). Within this study, Figure 8 shows one example of how this type of cutoff can bias the inferred cellular composition within this dataset.

10) It is unclear from the Materials and methods section how the clustering was done. The authors mention that "clusters were defined by a shared nearest neighbor method", but shared nearest neighbors is not a clustering algorithm. This is just an approach to constructing a graph from the data that can be used as input to a clustering algorithm. Was this graph used for Louvain community detection or something similar?

11) The authors identified a large number of clusters (120). Did all of these clusters have significant enrichment of distinct marker genes (e.g. based on the negative binomial test that the authors used)? What is the range in the number of cluster-specific markers associated with these clusters? Were certain clusters collapsed based on some criteria?

12) The authors state that they observed a median of 5 HD TFs per cell and 52 TFs in total per cell. These numbers may in large part reflect the indeterminate drop-out rate of the Chromium chemistry. It might be more meaningful to (additionally) report these numbers at the cluster level and also to state how many cluster-specific HDs or HD combinations were observed.

13) The single-cell expression correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B (and throughout) is complicated by transcript drop-out. The scatter plots in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D highlight the difficulty of assessing expression correlation at the single cell level from these data. Three different scatter plots that are quite visually similar are shown, but with very different correlation values that seem to be dependent on cell numbers. My guess is that cell numbers and expression levels significantly impact the correlation values at the single cell level. It would be interesting to check if the reported trends are consistent at the cluster level (e.g. by taking the average expression of all cells in each cluster and computing the correlation coefficients across clusters rather than across cells). It would also be worth doing this calculation separately for different replicates to determine their consistency, since this could be influenced by technical and coverage differences between replicates. This comment is not meant to challenge the overall validity of the authors' claims, which in some cases are orthogonally validated by immunostaining.

14) The analysis in Figure 4 is very compelling. There are many cells in the center of the tSNE plot that do not appear to correspond to any of the known lineage markers assessed in Figure 4 (in comparison to those in the periphery of the plot). These cells in the center are generally less tightly clustered. The authors specifically mention a large unc-4 expressing cholinergic cluster at the center of the plot, but Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows that this represents a relatively small fraction of the cells at the center. Is this phenomenon due to lower coverage cells clustering at the center of the tSNE plot (it is hard to tell from Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) or are these cells just biologically less distinct or require larger cell numbers to have sufficient coverage?

The manuscript has been greatly improved. There is one remaining issue that should be addressed before publication:

One reviewer was not convinced by Figure 5F that the cluster markers are segregated, as there seems to be co-labeled cell bodies across both clusters 23B and 8B. This is the only example where antibody staining or anatomical verification was used to confirm the accuracy of the cluster markers. I think it is worth quantifying the extent to which cells are co-labeled or adding labels to the images that make the result more clear.

results.result: The authors generated a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the adult Drosophila VNC using 10x Chromium chemistry, processing 80 VNCs (20 per replicate) and recovering 26,768 high-quality cells with a median of 1,170 genes and 2,497 transcripts per cell, representing more than 100 transcriptionally distinct cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C33, C34, C39, and C40 collectively describe the methodology and data generation. The experimental design with four replicates (C39), quality metrics (C40), and resulting atlas size (C4, C34) are clearly stated and internally consistent, providing strong support for this core methodological result.

results.result: The single-cell data showed high correlation with bulk VNC sequencing (r=0.76), high inter-replicate correlation (r=0.93-0.95), and cells from independent replicates were proportionally distributed across clusters with 94.6% alignment.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C42, C45, and C46 provide multiple lines of validation showing technical quality and reproducibility. The correlation values and alignment metrics are quantitative and consistent, demonstrating that the data are technically sound and replicates are well-integrated.

results.result: Using a cluster resolution of 12, the authors identified 120 distinct clusters, of which 110 were defined as neuronal based on expression of neuron-specific genes (elav, nSyb, noe), distinguished by differential expression of 1,205 cluster markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, C53, and C54 describe the clustering analysis and neuronal classification. The choice of resolution 12 is justified as best resolving established substructures (C43), and the use of established neuronal markers (C53) provides a principled basis for classification. The number of clusters and markers are clearly stated.

results.result: The 26,768 cells represent approximately 1.3-1.7x coverage of the adult VNC, based on comparison with prior estimates of 10,000-11,000 post-embryonic neurons, ~16,000 total cells, or ~20,000 cells from connectomic analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 provide coverage estimates based on multiple prior studies. The range of 1.3-1.7x coverage is calculated from different literature estimates (C49-C51), showing appropriate consideration of uncertainty in prior cell counts. The inference is reasonable given the cited references.

results.result: Immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSF) genes, including Dpr/DIP and Beat/Side subfamilies, were the most significantly enriched functional class among cluster markers, with Dpr/DIP genes marking over 50% of neuronal clusters and Beat/Side enrichment being largely mutually exclusive (80% of clusters enriched for either Beats or Sides).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 and C61-C63 describe IgSF enrichment with specific quantitative findings. The functional enrichment analysis (C55), continued expression in adults (C56), and mutually exclusive patterns (C62) are clearly stated. The inference about ongoing roles in connectivity maintenance (C63) is reasonable given the data, though speculative.

results.result: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) were significantly over-represented as cluster markers, with a median of 8 GPCRs per cell (12 at cluster level with 20% threshold), though generally expressed at low levels across many clusters, with neuropeptide receptors showing higher inter-cluster variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C69 describe GPCR expression patterns with specific quantitative metrics. The median values (C66, C67) and expression characteristics (C68) are clearly stated. The inference about neuropeptide receptor specialization (C69) is supported by the observed variation patterns.

results.result: Over 20% of Drosophila transcription factors (TFs) were cluster markers, with homeodomain (HD) TFs most enriched (median 6 HD TFs per cell, 10 at cluster level). Specific patterns included overlapping expression of Iro-C members ara/caup with independent mirr expression, and mutually exclusive LIM-HD TF expression, suggesting that developmental TF codes maintain neuronal identity in adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78, C81-C82, and C85 describe TF enrichment patterns with specific examples. The quantitative metrics (C75-C76), high variance (C77), and specific gene family patterns (C78, C81-C82) are clearly documented. The inference about maintenance of identity (C85) is reasonable given persistent expression of developmental TFs, though causality is not demonstrated.

results.result: Hox genes (Antp, Ubx, abd-A, Abd-B) define specific clusters with significantly anti-correlated expression patterns (except abd-A/Abd-B), validated by immunostaining showing neuromere-specific belts of expression along the anterior-posterior axis, allowing assignment of clusters to approximate neuromeres.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C98 describe Hox gene expression with both transcriptomic (C89-C92) and immunohistochemical validation (C93-C97). The anti-correlation patterns (C90) and spatial expression (C93-C97) are consistent and support the neuromere assignments (C98). The combination of single-cell and protein data strengthens this result.

results.result: Established lineage biomarkers showed continued expression in the adult VNC and were enriched as cluster markers, allowing assignment of potential hemilineage identities to many clusters. Cell counts within predicted hemilineages showed strong concordance with previous counts (r=0.89), further supporting ~1.5x VNC coverage.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C107 describe hemilineage annotation using established markers. The continued expression of developmental markers (C101), assignment methodology (C102-C103), and validation through cell count correlation (C106) provide strong support. The example of cluster 54 as hemilineage 9B (C104) illustrates the approach.

results.result: Novel hemilineage markers were identified, including 34 TFs (approximately half with homeodomains) and 5 lncRNAs among the 59 most enriched genes. Two lncRNAs (MRE23, CR45141) are divergently transcribed from protein-coding genes (fkh, vg) and show correlated expression, suggesting shared cis-regulatory landscapes.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 and C121-C122 describe novel markers with specific quantitative details. The identification of lncRNAs (C119), their genomic organization (C121), and expression correlation (C122) are clearly documented. The inference about shared regulation (C122) is reasonable given divergent transcription patterns.

results.result: Many predicted hemilineages contain multiple clusters representing variations based on birth order and anatomical position. Expression of br marks cells born around L2-L3 ecdysis, while pros and Imp show negative correlation, with pros labeling late-born post-embryonic neurons and Imp labeling early-born/embryonic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C131 and C137 describe hemilineage subdivisions with specific marker patterns. The br expression (C126-C127), pros/Imp anti-correlation (C129), and anatomical biases (C131) are documented. The inference about birth order (C137) is supported by cited developmental studies (C134-C136), though direct validation in this dataset is limited.

results.result: Hemilineage 23B contains four distinct clusters, with novel markers kn and twz enriched in independent clusters (51 and 93). Immunohistochemical validation confirmed that 34% of 23B cells are kn+ and 21% are twz+, consistent with single-cell data (31% and 18%), while Lim3 expression was restricted to hemilineages 8B/9B (90% co-expression with Acj6, 0% in 23B).
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C143, C146-C149, and C151 provide a complete example of marker discovery and validation. The single-cell predictions (C142) are validated by immunostaining (C143, C146-C149) with quantitative agreement between methods (C148). This demonstrates the predictive power of the atlas (C151).

results.result: Fast-acting neurotransmitter (FAN) markers (VAChT, VGlut, Gad1) showed mutually exclusive enrichment at the cluster level, though 31% of cells expressed at least two markers. FAN identity was assigned by cluster-level average expression, estimating the VNC as 40% cholinergic, 38% GABAergic, and 18% glutamatergic.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C156 and C161-C163 describe FAN classification. The cluster-level exclusivity (C153) contrasts with cell-level co-expression (C156), which is addressed by using cluster-level assignment (C161). The proportions (C163) differ from brain estimates, which is noted. However, the high co-expression rate raises questions about ambient RNA contamination (C160).

results.result: Co-expression of FAN markers observed in single-cell data may represent ambient RNA contamination, as immunostaining of intact VNC suggested no cytoplasmic co-expression and nuclear transcriptomic profiles from visual system and mushroom body found no evidence for FAN co-release.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C160 address a technical concern about FAN co-expression. The contrast between single-cell data and immunostaining (C158) and nuclear profiling (C159) supports the ambient RNA hypothesis (C160). This is an important technical consideration that affects interpretation of C156.

results.result: The VNC has a higher proportion of GABAergic neurons (38%) compared to the adult midbrain (15%), and the inhibitory glutamate receptor GluClα is enriched in cluster 103, suggesting that inhibitory signaling is prominent in the VNC, reflecting its importance in motor program coordination.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C166 describe the prominence of inhibitory signaling. The comparison to brain (C164), GluClα expression (C165), and functional inference (C166) are clearly stated. The inference about motor coordination (C166) is reasonable given VNC function, though speculative.

results.result: Sub-clustering of Vmat+ cells identified distinct monoaminergic populations (histaminergic, octopaminergic, dopaminergic, serotonergic) based on biosynthetic markers. Novel markers were identified for each subtype, including Frq1 and CG43795 for HA neurons, beat-Ib/Ic and Toll-6 for DA neurons, and 5-HT1A and JhI-21 for 5-HT neurons, suggesting auto-regulation and amino acid sensing.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C186 describe monoaminergic neuron characterization. The sub-clustering approach (C167), replicate consistency (C168), and identification of novel markers for each subtype (C171, C178, C181, C185) are well-documented. The functional inferences about auto-regulation (C184) and amino acid sensing (C186) are reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Each monoaminergic subtype expresses unique combinations of homeodomain TFs: otp/Lmx1a for HA, hth/mirr for DA, and vvl/ey/Lim3 for 5-HT neurons. These TFs likely specify developmental patterning and may contribute to mature neuron function.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C191 describe TF codes for monoaminergic subtypes. The specific combinations (C188-C190) are clearly documented. The inference about developmental and functional roles (C191) is reasonable but speculative, as functional validation is not provided.

results.result: 28 neuropeptides are expressed in the VNC (≥10 transcripts per cell), with some showing FAN-specific associations (sNPF/spab in cholinergic, MIP/CCHa2 in GABAergic, Ilp7/Proc in glutamatergic neurons). Some associations differ from midbrain data, notably AstC/CCHa2 are robustly expressed in VNC GABAergic neurons but absent from midbrain Gad1+ neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C198 describe neuropeptide expression patterns. The identification of 28 neuropeptides (C193), FAN associations (C195), and regional differences (C197-C198) are clearly documented. The comparison to midbrain highlights VNC-specific features.

results.result: Cluster 84 exhibits neurosecretory characteristics, including enrichment for dimm (10.7% vs 0.03% elsewhere), high neuropeptide expression with non-overlapping subsets, expression of neuropeptide processing genes, and lack of FAN markers. Gpa2 and Gpb5, which form heterodimers, are co-expressed in this cluster.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C206 characterize cluster 84 as neurosecretory. The dimm enrichment (C202), neuropeptide expression patterns (C203, C205), processing gene expression (C204), and Gpa2/Gpb5 co-expression (C206) collectively support this classification. The low dimm detection is noted but explained by the bias to cluster 84.

results.result: Neuropeptide-expressing cluster 84 has a median of 5,277 transcripts per cell (vs 2,497 overall), due to high neuropeptide gene expression. Leucokinin reached 2,629 transcripts in a single cell, 18 of the top 40 most highly expressed genes encode neuropeptides, and all 28 expressed neuropeptide genes exceeded the 93rd percentile (23/28 above 99th percentile), sometimes representing 40% of cellular transcriptional output.
results.evaluation: Claims C207-C213 document exceptionally high neuropeptide expression with specific quantitative metrics. The median transcript counts (C207), maximum expression levels (C209), ranking (C210-C211), and proportional contribution (C212) are clearly stated. The comparison to mouse cortex (C213) provides cross-species context.

results.result: The 10,000 transcript upper filtering cutoff excluded many neuropeptide and Proctolin+ motor neuron cluster cells. Removing this cutoff revealed cells exceeding 10,000 transcripts, with Orcokinin reaching 23,092 transcripts maximum. This highlights the importance of considering filtering thresholds when studying high-expression cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C214-C217 address a technical consideration about filtering. The identification of cells exceeding the threshold (C215), extreme example (C217), and methodological recommendation (C216) are clearly stated. This is an important technical point for future studies.

results.result: Orcokinin is expressed in 5 neurons in the adult VNC, with 5 cells in the NP cluster showing >100 transcripts, but ~8,000 cells across all clusters showing 1-10 transcripts. This pattern suggests that low-level expression represents ambient RNA contamination from ruptured high-expressing cells, while >100 transcripts represents bona fide expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C218-C222 use Orcokinin as an example of ambient RNA contamination. The known expression pattern (C219), observed high expression (C220), widespread low expression (C221), and interpretation (C222) are clearly documented. This provides a specific example of the technical issue raised in C218.

results.result: Five clusters (3.6% of cells) were identified as glial based on repo and MRE16 expression and lack of neuronal markers. Sub-clustering revealed four glial subpopulations: astrocytes (alrm+), surface glia (Indy+), cortex glia (wrapper+), and ensheathing glia (Eaat2+).
results.evaluation: Claims C224-C228 describe glial cell identification and classification. The use of established markers (C224), proportion of cells (C225), lack of neuronal markers (C226), and sub-clustering with established markers (C228) provide a clear classification scheme. The mixed populations (C227) are appropriately handled by removing neuronal-signature cells.

results.result: Surface glia, which form the blood-brain barrier, strongly express sugar transporters (Tret1-1, CG4797) and are enriched for V-type ATPase H+ pumping genes, bicarbonate transporter CG8177, and ImpL2 (which antagonizes insulin signaling), suggesting metabolic responsiveness to fly demands.
results.evaluation: Claims C229-C236 characterize surface glia function. The expression of transporters (C231-C232), proton pumps (C234), pH regulators (C235), and insulin antagonist (C236) are documented with functional context. The inference about metabolic responsiveness (C236) is reasonable given the gene expression patterns.

results.result: Over 70% of VNC astrocyte markers are shared with midbrain astrocytes, suggesting minimal regional specialization. Despite astrocytes and ensheathing glia sharing developmental lineages with motor neurons, no lineage-specific transcriptional code was found. Instead, astrocytes express CG34367 and ensheathing glia express vvl, consistent with morphological plasticity rather than distinct TF codes.
results.evaluation: Claims C237-C244 describe glial transcriptional identity. The marker overlap (C237), lack of lineage-specific code (C240), and identification of cell-type-specific TFs (C241-C243) are clearly documented. The interpretation about plasticity vs. TF codes (C244) is supported by cited developmental studies.

results.result: Two clusters represent contamination: cluster 99 is salivary gland tissue (8 of top 10 genes match FlyAtlas 2 salivary gland markers) and cluster 116 is sperm (markers unique to testis/sperm).
results.evaluation: Claims C245-C247 identify contaminating cell types. The use of tissue-specific markers from FlyAtlas 2 (C246) and testis/sperm markers (C247) provides clear evidence for contamination. This is an important quality control observation.

results.result: The predominant gene signatures defining neuronal cell types reflect shared developmental histories based on neuroblast origin and birth order, with maintained expression of Hox and neuronal lineage marker genes persisting in the adult.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C37 state a major conclusion about developmental signatures in adult transcriptomes. This is supported by the extensive documentation of Hox gene expression (C86-C98), lineage marker persistence (C100-C107), and TF code maintenance (C74-C85). The conclusion is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: The relative position of cells along the anterior-posterior axis can be assigned using adult Hox gene expression, allowing separation of clusters into neuromere approximations.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C98 describe spatial assignment using Hox genes. This is supported by the anti-correlation patterns (C90), immunostaining validation (C93-C97), and the combination of these data to assign neuromeres (C98). The approach is sound and validated.

results.result: The VNC has roughly equal numbers of inhibitory GABAergic (38%) and excitatory cholinergic (40%) neurons, with 18% glutamatergic and 4% undefined.
results.evaluation: Claims C35 and C163 state FAN proportions. While C35 says "roughly equal" and C163 gives specific percentages showing slight cholinergic predominance, the values are close enough to support the general claim. The methodology for assignment (C161) is described, though concerns about ambient RNA (C160) should be noted.

results.result: Genes encoding preproneuropeptides are amongst the most highly expressed in the VNC, with 28 neuropeptides expressed at ≥10 transcripts per cell, 18 of the top 40 most highly expressed genes encoding neuropeptides, and all 28 above the 93rd percentile.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C193, and C207-C211 document high neuropeptide expression. The quantitative metrics (C209-C211) strongly support the claim that neuropeptides are among the most highly expressed genes (C36). This is a clear and well-supported finding.

results.result: The single-cell profiles provide many novel markers for known and new cell types, with predictive power demonstrated by validation of kn and twz as hemilineage 23B subtype markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C117, and C151 describe the discovery of novel markers. The identification of novel hemilineage markers (C117) and their validation (C142-C149) demonstrate the predictive power (C151). This is a key utility of the atlas.
